FAQ.heading: Frequently asked questions
FAQ.subheading: What people usually ask before linking an account, and what's worth knowing about what Paragon can and can't do.

general.q1: Do I have to give you my PlayStation or Steam password?
general.a1: No, and there's no way to even if you wanted to — there's no field for it. Paragon reads public profiles with a server credential. Linking an account is just saying "that's me", the same as typing your username.
general.q2: Why does my library show up empty?
general.a2: It's almost always a privacy setting on the source platform. On PSN, your trophy profile has to be public. On Steam you need two settings, not one: "My Profile" and "Game Details", both public. If you only set the profile, the API returns an empty library without any error.
general.q3: How often does the data update?
general.a3: Linking an account imports everything at once, and from then on you can force a refresh anytime with "Sync now" in settings. A specific game's achievements are pulled the first time you open its page.

plataformas.a1: PlayStation (PSN) and Steam, both in full: games, achievements, rarity percentages and progress. On Steam we also read developer, publisher and genres, which is what lets you group your library by company.
plataformas.q2: What about Google Play Games or Apple Game Center?
plataformas.a2: It's not possible, and it's not a matter of time or effort. The Google Play Games API only returns achievements for games that belong to your own developer project: there's no endpoint to read a player's achievements in third-party games, not even with their permission. Game Center is even more closed off: GameKit only works on-device and only for your own game, with no server API.
plataformas.a3: Xbox is doable, but its official API is partner-only; it would need to rely on a third-party middleman. Epic and GOG don't publish an achievements API, so any integration would depend on unofficial endpoints that can break without warning.
plataformas.q4: Why aren't there platinums on Steam?
plataformas.a4: Because Steam has no metal tiers: an achievement is an achievement and they all count the same. Bronze, silver, gold and platinum are PlayStation's. That's why on Steam games the equivalent of finishing something is reaching 100%, shown as "At 100%" instead of "Platinumed".

biblioteca.a1: Groupings you build by hand ("2026 backlog", "For summer"). They exist because automatic grouping by company depends on the platform telling us who publishes each game, and PSN doesn't. You create and fill them from any game's page.
biblioteca.q2: Why don't some PSN games show a company?
biblioteca.a2: Because the PlayStation API doesn't expose developer or publisher. Steam's does. Covering PSN games would mean cross-referencing titles with an external catalog, which brings its own matching errors. Folders exist for that in the meantime.
biblioteca.a3: By pending achievements, not percentage. A game at 90% with fifty achievements leaves you more work than one at 70% with ten. Finished games and ones you haven't started are left out, since "what's left" doesn't tell you anything in either case.
biblioteca.a4: The score you give a game counts toward the community average shown on its page, next to the vote count. The average and the count always go together on purpose: a 5.0 with one vote doesn't say the same thing as a 4.2 with forty.

f1.titulo: What's missing, not what you have
f1.cuerpo: Every game is sorted by the trophies you have left, with the one most people earn at the top. The platinum comes last: it's the result, not the task.

f2.cuerpo: Only the games you have in common, bar against bar. Compare with one friend or several at once, like a clan.

f3.cuerpo: You type your public PlayStation ID and that's it. Nobody hands over passwords or tokens, and we don't store anyone's secrets.

f4.titulo: The Wrap, backed by a leaderboard
f4.cuerpo: Your most-played genre, your most-squeezed game, your trophies of the year — and each one links to the full leaderboard, with a date filter.

f5.cuerpo: The platinum's real rarity and what people who already earned it think, side by side. Neither one lies on its own.

f6.cuerpo: A new trophy, the moment you unlock it, straight to your phone or browser — no need to open the app to find out.

f7.cuerpo: Full screen with your nearest trophies, big buttons and a video guide. For when you already know what you're platinuming today.

f8.cuerpo: XP for every trophy and for completing games, badges for milestones, and a monthly league that starts from zero for everyone every month.

ComoFunciona.descripcion: Everything Paragon does, explained for real — not a list of headlines, but what each thing does and where to find it.

vincular.b1: You type your public identifier (your PSN ID, your SteamID64/profile URL, or your Gamertag) — never a password, there isn't even a field for it. On PSN your trophy profile has to be public; on Steam you need two settings public at once ("My profile" and "Game details"). Xbox uses an unofficial third-party service (OpenXBL) — it can break if that service changes, it doesn't depend on Microsoft.
vincular.b2t: Which platforms can't be linked yet
vincular.b2: Epic Games, Google Play and Ubisoft Connect have been removed from the selector — none of them currently has a real way in (a documented public API) to read third-party trophies. It's not a Paragon limitation, it's that those platforms don't allow it without reverse-engineering their internal API.
vincular.b3: A cron job goes through linked accounts and pulls in what's new on its own, without you having to log in. On top of that, every time you open a game's page it checks whether it needs refreshing.
vincular.b4: A manual button in the header (and in Settings → Game Accounts) to force an immediate sync, with a cooldown so it doesn't hit the source APIs more than it needs to.

trofeos.b1: Every game is sorted by pending trophies, with the easiest to earn at the top — the platinum is the result of finishing the list, not the task itself.
trofeos.b2: Trophies you can permanently miss if you don't grab them in time, pulled from real PowerPyx guides — with a curated list of alternate titles for games PowerPyx calls something else (checked one by one, not a generic rule that guesses wrong).
trofeos.b3: Click any trophy in the list and it searches YouTube for a guide on its own — cached at the trophy level (the first search covers everyone), with a "Not this one — find another" button if the video isn't right.
trofeos.b4: On that same trophy page, a written-guide tab that any Paragon user can fill in — with external search links (Google, IGN, GameFAQs) if there isn't one yet.
trofeos.b5: For trophies the platform doesn't break down either ("win 50 matches", "find 100 items") — you set the target and track it with two buttons, right on the trophy page.
trofeos.b6: Filter the list by Missable, Multiplayer, Collectibles, Story, Skill or Secret. The "Tree" view visually connects related trophies — a reading aid, not a real fact about what unlocks what (neither PSN nor Steam exposes that).
trofeos.b7: Community story and completionist hours from HLTB, on the game's page and in the Planner — the average across everyone, not a personalized promise.
trofeos.b8: Full screen with your nearest trophies and big buttons, for when you already know what you're platinuming today and don't want distractions.

estadisticas.b1: A single score that weighs every trophy by its real rarity (and by Gamerscore on Xbox) — that's what your Paragon level and progress toward the next one are built from.
estadisticas.b2: Automatic milestones (your first platinum, streaks, trophy volume…) that unlock on their own once the condition is met, nothing to claim by hand.
estadisticas.b3: A little square per day for trophies earned (GitHub-style), plus a second map crossing day of the week with hour of the day — when you actually play, not just which days.
estadisticas.b4: A radar chart by genre (Action, RPG, Adventure, Strategy, Platformer, Puzzle, Sports) weighted by trophies you've actually earned, not your whole library — with an archetype assigned based on your strongest category.
estadisticas.b5: Your first platinum, your rarest trophy, the "vintage platinum" (the one that took longest from first trophy to platinum), and your longest streak of consecutive days.
estadisticas.b6: You enter what you paid for a game and where it's from (physical, digital, PS Plus, Game Pass, borrowed, free) on its page, and Paragon works out the $/hour using your real playtime — nothing made up, just what you entered yourself.
estadisticas.b7: The % of people who have each game's platinum (or its rarest trophy, if there's no platinum) translated into a difficulty scale — a real rarity figure, not an opinion score.
estadisticas.b8: Everything above together on the "Stats" tab of your profile, plus hours in perspective, monthly charts and comparisons with your friends.

backlog.b1: Games with a lot of progress (75%+) that haven't been touched in months — a reminder that they're there, one push away from platinum.
backlog.b2: Games in your library with not a single hour, not a single trophy — with a "Blind play" button that picks one at random and gives you a 2-hour trial.
backlog.b3: Say how much time you have (and which genre, if you want) and it suggests "quick wins" (few real trophies left to grab) and "go deeper" games (based on HLTB hours minus what you've already played). It shuffles among the most relevant ones, so it doesn't always repeat the same picks.
backlog.b4: Catalog by platform, trends, upcoming releases and recommendations based on what you already play — for when you don't know what to add to your wishlist.
backlog.b5: Mark any game as wanted from its page or from Discover — it doesn't count as "your game" in any stat until you actually own it.
backlog.b6: Releases and updates from PlayStation, Xbox and Steam, pulled from each platform's public sources.

comunidad.b1: What your friends are up to — platinums, reviews, comments — in one place, with reactions and replies.
comunidad.b2: Rate and write about any game you own, visible on your public profile and on the game's page for everyone.
comunidad.b3: Guides written by any user about a whole game (as opposed to a guide for ONE trophy — see the Trophies tab), with replies from other users.
comunidad.b4: Only the games you have in common, bar against bar — with one friend or several at once, like a clan.
comunidad.b5: Send and accept friend requests, and compare trophy, platinum and playtime rankings within your group.
comunidad.b6: A ranking that starts from zero for everyone every month — however long you've been playing, everyone starts equal on day 1.

planificador.b1: Organize the order you'll platinum your backlog in, with HLTB estimated hours broken down into story and platinum — plus a dropdown to sort by "fastest" when data is available.
planificador.b2: Trophies per month, your current streak and your best-ever streak, and a summary of your activity over time.
planificador.b3: A "Spotify Wrapped"-style recap of your year in trophies — your most-played genre, your most-squeezed game, your trophies of the year — in a Stories format with a link to the real leaderboard behind every figure.
planificador.b4: Small goals that reset every week (earn X trophies, try a new game…) — optional, with no reward beyond the streak itself.

notificaciones.b1: A direct alert to your phone or browser the moment you unlock a trophy — turn it on from Settings. On iPhone you need to install Paragon via "Share → Add to Home Screen" in Safari for it to work (an Apple limitation, not Paragon's).
notificaciones.b2: Turn on Paragon bot DM alerts from Settings — it needs you to have signed in with Discord. From then on you get the same things by DM that already arrive by push: friend requests, level-ups from people around you, and league invites.
notificaciones.b3t: Add the bot to your server
notificaciones.b3ConLink: Anyone can invite it with this link — <link>add Paragon to a Discord server →</link> — Discord will ask which server and to confirm the permissions (it only asks for <enviarMensajes>Send Messages</enviarMensajes>, so it can post in the <comando>/anunciosaqui</comando> channel). You don't need to own the server, just "Manage Server" permission there.
notificaciones.b3LinkTexto: add Paragon to a Discord server →
notificaciones.b3SinConfigurar: Bot being set up — check back later.
notificaciones.cmdPerfil: your Paragon stats, or a friend's if they've linked Discord.
notificaciones.cmdRacha: your current streak of consecutive days earning at least one trophy.
notificaciones.cmdPlatinosalalcance: heavily-progressed games that have sat untouched for months — your nearby-platinums radar.
notificaciones.cmdVerguenza: the Hall of Shame: games with not a single hour, not a single trophy.
notificaciones.cmdJuego: a quick summary of a game in your library (length, difficulty, missables, your progress).
notificaciones.cmdNota: jot a private note on a game without opening the site.
notificaciones.cmdHoy: what you can finish off today based on the time and genre you're in the mood for.
notificaciones.cmdRuleta: picks a backlog game that fits the time you have.
notificaciones.cmdLigas: your leagues with friends and your standing in each one.
notificaciones.cmdLiga: the full standings of a league (name doesn't need to be exact) and its challenge, if it has one.
notificaciones.cmdInvitacionesliga: league invites you haven't accepted or declined yet.
notificaciones.b6ConComando: Anyone with manage-server permission can type <comando>/anunciosaqui</comando> in whatever channel they want — from then on, the bot posts right there whenever someone from the server levels up in Paragon (only to people who have alerts turned on in Paragon, and only if they're still actually in that server). Only one channel can be active per server — running the command again in another channel moves the destination, it doesn't add to it.
notificaciones.b7ConComando: The <comando>/help</comando> command lists every bot command from inside Discord, without coming back to this page.

perfil.b1: Banner, accent color, avatar frame (based on your Paragon level), a custom title and status, and the order of your profile's sections, your way.
perfil.b2: Group your games into folders by hand, and pin up to 3 trophies in a featured showcase on your profile.
perfil.b3: A reminder only you can see ("still need collectible 14 in chapter 3") — never public, unlike a review.
perfil.b4: Remove the features you don't care about from the menu (Community, Leagues, Friends, Discover, News, Planner) — just for you, they keep existing for everyone else.
perfil.b5: Dark, light, OLED or high contrast, plus a free accent color — applied before the page paints, no flicker.
perfil.b6ConLinks: What data we ask for and why, with no third-party analytics or advertising — see also <cookies>Cookies</cookies> and <terminos>Terms</terminos>.
perfil.b7ConLink: Download a JSON of everything Paragon knows about you, from Settings → Login and Security. To delete your account entirely, that's currently handled by email — see <privacidad>Privacy</privacidad>.

Privacidad.s1: Paragon is a personal project by Mario García, not a company. Under the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), Mario García is the data controller for the processing described here. You can write to mario.meca2005@gmail.com with any question or to exercise your rights (section 6).
Privacidad.s2intro: Only what's needed for the service to work:
Privacidad.s2li1: When you create your account: the name, email and profile picture that Google or Discord give us when you sign in with them (they're the only two sign-in providers; Paragon never sees or stores your password for those services).
Privacidad.s2li2: When you link a gaming platform (PlayStation, Steam, Xbox, and any others that can genuinely be linked in the future): your public identifier on that platform, and the data that platform makes public alongside it — game library, trophies or achievements, hours played and level. It's read with server credentials, never with yours: linking means saying "that's me over there", not granting access to your account.
Privacidad.s2li3: Content you write: reviews, private notes per game, guides, comments, your handle, and whatever you customize on your public profile (title, banner, color, etc.).
Privacidad.s2li4: Push notifications (optional): if you turn on browser alerts in Settings, we store the "endpoint" your own browser generates so it can send you that notification — it's not data that identifies you personally, your browser (Chrome/Firefox/etc.) generates it and it's only used for that.
Privacidad.s2li5: Discord webhook (optional): if you paste a webhook URL from your own Discord server to receive trophy alerts there, that URL is stored exactly as you typed it. Only you can see it, and it's only used to send the messages you asked for.
Privacidad.s3li1: Letting you log in and manage your account.
Privacidad.s3li2: Calculating and showing your trophy, achievement and progress stats.
Privacidad.s3li3: Comparisons with friends, the community feed and leagues.
Privacidad.s3li4: Sending you the push or Discord alerts you turned on yourself.
Privacidad.s3p: We never sell, rent or share your personal data with third parties for commercial or advertising purposes. Paragon doesn't show ads or use third-party advertising. We do measure aggregated, anonymous visits with Vercel Analytics (no cookies, no identifying you — see the cookie policy for exactly what it measures).
Privacidad.s4t: Who it's shared with, and why
Privacidad.s4intro: None of your data is sold. There are technical services that process it for us, or that we read public data from:
Privacidad.s4li1: Vercel hosts the application. Supabase hosts the database. Both act as data processors, not as owners of your data.
Privacidad.s4li2: Google and Discord, only for sign-in (OAuth) — they don't receive trophy data or your activity on Paragon.
Privacidad.s4li3: PlayStation Network, Steam and Xbox (the last one via an unofficial third-party service): your public trophy data is read from there, nothing is ever sent to them.
Privacidad.s4li4: IGDB, PowerPyx, HowLongToBeat, YouTube and IsThereAnyDeal: sources we read public information about the games themselves from (covers, genres, guides, completion times, prices) — they don't receive your data, we only ask them for information about a game.
Privacidad.s4li5: Your own browser's push notification service (for example Firebase Cloud Messaging on Chrome), only if you turn on alerts — it's the web's standard mechanism, not something Paragon-specific.
Privacidad.s5: For as long as your account exists. If you delete it (section 6), your linked platform accounts, private notes, push subscription and Discord webhook get deleted along with it. Public content you've shared with other people (reviews, comments, guides) may be anonymized instead of fully deleted, if deleting it entirely would break someone else's conversation.
Privacidad.s6: Access, rectification, erasure, portability, objection and restriction of processing — the full GDPR list. You can download a copy of your own data from <ajustesLink>Settings → Login and Security</ajustesLink>. To delete your account, or for any other right, write to <email>mario.meca2005@gmail.com</email> — you'll get a response within 30 days, the deadline GDPR sets. You can also file a complaint with the Spanish Data Protection Agency (aepd.es) if you feel your request wasn't handled.
Privacidad.s7: Paragon never asks for or stores passwords for your PlayStation, Steam, Xbox or any other gaming platform accounts. Syncing uses public identifiers, never private Sony, Valve or Microsoft credentials.
Privacidad.s8: Paragon isn't directed at children under 14 and doesn't knowingly request data from anyone under that age. If you believe a minor has given us data, let us know and we'll remove it.
Privacidad.s9: If this policy changes in a meaningful way, the date above will be updated and, when the change matters, you'll be notified inside the app itself.

Cookies.s1: Paragon doesn't use advertising or analytics cookies. There's no tracking pixel, no Google Analytics, no embedded social widgets that could follow you around. There's just one cookie, and it's the one that keeps you logged in — the usage analytics we do measure (see below) uses no cookies and doesn't identify you.
Cookies.s2: When you sign in with Google or Discord, Paragon stores a technical cookie (managed by Auth.js) that identifies your session so you don't have to log in again on every page. It's strictly necessary for the app to work — without it, an account can't stay logged in — which is why it doesn't ask for separate consent: cookie regulations (the ePrivacy Directive's Spanish transposition, LSSI-CE) exempt strictly necessary technical or operational cookies.
Cookies.s3: Some preferences — your color theme, font size, or whether you've already closed this cookie notice — are stored with <localStorage>localStorage</localStorage> in your own browser, not in a cookie or on our servers. They stay only on your device, they don't travel with every request the way a cookie does, and you can clear them anytime from your browser's settings.
Cookies.s4: Since September 2026 we measure aggregated visits (which pages get viewed, approximate country, device type) with <vercelLink>Vercel Analytics</vercelLink>. It uses no cookies — it identifies each visit with an anonymous hash that's discarded after 24 hours, not a permanent identifier tied to you — and it doesn't cross data with any other site, which is why this doesn't require consent. We don't know which specific games you look at through this — that comes from your logged-in account, not from analytics.
Cookies.s5: If Paragon ever adds advertising or any non-essential cookie in the future, we'll ask for your explicit consent before turning it on and this page will be updated to explain it.
Cookies.s6: To see what personal data is processed and why, check the <privacidadLink>Privacy Policy</privacidadLink> and the <terminosLink>Terms and Conditions</terminosLink>.
